source: Kaufman, Brun, Murali, Endres (2026) Programmers Are Poor and Overconfident Judges of LLM-Generated Assertions
finding: Humans judging LLM-written postconditions are far better at accepting correct ones than rejecting wrong ones, yet equally confident in both.
numbers: Controlled experiment, 86 programmers (after exclusions from 106 submissions; mean age 27.1; 66.3% professionals). Correct postconditions judged correct 73.9%; incorrect ones caught only 49.0% (p<0.001).
quote: participants were much better at identifying correct assertions than identifying incorrect ones
limits: Python HumanEval-style functions; online survey; exploratory coding of strategies.
agent_relevance: The agent must not trust an accepted-looking reading of code or spec. Accept bias is human and probably model-like; S1/S2 reading needs a check that can reject (run an example).

source: Kaufman, Brun, Murali, Endres (2026) Programmers Are Poor and Overconfident Judges of LLM-Generated Assertions (think-aloud strategy coding)
finding: Think-aloud study coded each response as top-down, bottom-up or as-needed (the von Mayrhauser and Vans labels). Top-down dominated when a docstring was present.
numbers: 10 think-aloud participants, 50 responses: top-down 31/50 (62%), bottom-up 7/50 (14%), as-needed 10/50 (20%), undetermined 2/50. Five reasoning strategies: clause comparison, logic walk-through, positive example, negative example, intuition.
limits: Small N; spec-vs-code task, not free exploration of an unknown code base; two authors coded.
agent_relevance: When a spec or comment exists, humans read it first and confirm in code. An agent can copy this: state expectation from the spec, then verify bottom-up. Intuition-only answers were wrong 7/12 times, so S1 should ban verdicts without a trace or example.

source: Kaufman, Brun, Murali, Endres (2026) Programmers Are Poor and Overconfident Judges of LLM-Generated Assertions (reasoning strategy and accuracy)
finding: Negative examples were used mostly to confirm a suspected error; intuition was the weakest strategy. Easy items allowed clause comparison.
numbers: Intuition used in 12/50 responses, 7/12 wrong, making up most of the 11 incorrect responses. 18/29 perceived-incorrect responses used negative examples (14/18 to confirm an earlier hunch). Clause comparison used by every participant on 4 of the 5 items with >=75% accuracy.
limits: Think-aloud N=10.
agent_relevance: Supports a rule: after any plausible reading, force a counterexample attempt (try to break it) before accepting.

source: Lehmen, Wyrich, Maurer, Peitek, Apel (2026) Predicting Program Comprehension with Foundation Models of Human Cognition
finding: Centaur (Llama 3.1 fine-tuned on 160 psychology experiments) predicts human responses on 9 published program-comprehension studies better than base Llama 3.1.
numbers: Mean negative log likelihood 1.63 (Centaur) vs 1.85 (Llama); p<0.001; effect size 0.172 (small). Centaur better in 7 of 9 studies (2 negligible, 4 small, 1 medium); 1 no difference, 1 slightly worse. 9 studies chosen from 95 articles via a 5-step filter (33 -> 19 -> 15 -> 9).
limits: Only 9 datasets with short text answers; free-text studies were hard for both models (neg. log lik >4.0); models predict response distributions, not mental processes.
agent_relevance: Models carry some generic human response regularities, but the gain is small. Do not treat the model as a stand-in for a human reader; keep the checks in code.

source: Lehmen, Wyrich, Maurer, Peitek, Apel (2026) Predicting Program Comprehension with Foundation Models of Human Cognition (ablations)
finding: Centaur's gain comes from better response-format alignment and from using the task description and code; Llama leans more on prior-trial answers.
numbers: Ablations over seven prompt variants (CODE, DESC, SEQU removed). Code removal hurt Centaur more in S2, S3, S4, Llama more in S5, S6, S7. Removing the task description gave a small consistent hit to Centaur in almost all studies (exception S7).
limits: Effects differ by study; no stated process-level reading of bottom-up vs top-down.
agent_relevance: Prior answers in context bias a base model more than the code itself does. For the agent: do not show earlier verdicts when asking for a fresh reading.

source: Li, Zhang, Karas, Leach, Huang, McMillan (2024) Do Machines and Humans Focus on Similar Code? Explainability of LLMs in Code Summarization
finding: Where six code models focus (SHAP) does not line up with where 27 programmers look (eye tracking) when summarizing Java methods.
numbers: 27 programmers, 671 eye-tracking trials, 68 methods. At most 22% of methods had a significant human-model Spearman correlation; 85% of methods had significant correlation between pairs of models. Alignment vs summary quality: accuracy rho -0.128 (p=0.386), completeness 0.131, conciseness 0.019, readability -0.072; all n.s. Models focus more on comments, returns, literals, assignments; less on method calls.
quote: we find no statistically significant evidence suggesting the hypothesized alignment
limits: Java summarization only; SHAP may be a weak attribution method; low power.
agent_relevance: The model's reading path is not the human reading path. Do not assume model reading mimics beacons-first human reading. Make the agent's read order explicit in the scaffold.

source: Paltenghi, Pandita, Henley, Ziegler (2022/2024) Follow-up Attention: Developer and Neural Model Code Exploration
finding: Model attention partly matches developer eye-gaze on code-sensemaking questions, and models answer far worse than developers.
numbers: 25 developers, 92 valid sessions (~19 min), 45 tasks (5 snippets x 3 questions x Python/C++/C#). Developers correct or partly correct ~70%; CodeGen 39.3%, InCoder 37.7%, GPT-J 36.3%. Visual-attention Spearman with developers: CodeGen +0.22, InCoder +0.20, GPT-J +0.04.
limits: One company; sensemaking tasks not real debugging; small 2022-era models; prompt-dependent.
agent_relevance: Early evidence that raw code models read code differently from people. The paradigm (question about snippet, then trace what is read) can be reused to test our scaffold's S1.

source: Paltenghi, Pandita, Henley, Ziegler (2022/2024) Follow-up Attention: Developer and Neural Model Code Exploration (next-line prediction)
finding: Post-processing attention into 'follow-up attention' predicts the next line a developer looks at, better than position or copy heuristics.
numbers: Top-3 line overlap 47% vs 42.3% for a baseline using another developer's session. Developer-to-developer navigation-path agreement +0.56; follow-up attention +0.49. Agreement higher for C# than Python.
quote: Our follow-up attention method can predict the next line a developer will look at with 47% accuracy.
limits: Small gain over the peer baseline; early layers did well; memorization possible.
agent_relevance: Navigation order is predictable from model internals, which hints that an agent could be steered along a human-like path (call chain, then next callee). Weak evidence.

source: Alebachew (2025) AI-Guided Exploration of Large-Scale Codebases
finding: Prototype tool using an LLM planner and AST-derived UML to guide code exploration, justified by information foraging and cognitive load theory. No evaluation yet.
numbers: No user study, no measured results. Cites that developers spend up to 70% of time on program comprehension.
limits: Java only; claims of generality unproven.
agent_relevance: Shows the design idea (deterministic parse + LLM only chooses where to look) that matches our rule 'program decides, model fills slot'. No effect size to lean on.

source: Qiao, Shihab, Hundhausen (2025) A Systematic Literature Review of GenAI Assistants for Code Comprehension
finding: Review of 31 papers (2022-2024) on GenAI for code comprehension; restates the bottom-up (novice) vs top-down (expert, via beacons) split as the frame.
numbers: 3,930 unique papers screened -> 58 eligible -> 74 after snowballing -> 31 after quality filter. Comprehension takes ~52-70% of maintenance time.
limits: Education-leaning; most primary studies are tool demos with small samples.
agent_relevance: Confirms that the field mostly tests tools, not the strategy models themselves; little direct test of von Mayrhauser and Vans with LLMs.

source: Qiao, Shihab, Hundhausen (2025) A Systematic Literature Review of GenAI Assistants for Code Comprehension (explanation effectiveness)
finding: Anchored AI explanations raised comprehension-question accuracy; LLM explanations still contain errors.
numbers: Ivie study: 90.2% correct vs 65.0% for a baseline in-editor chatbot (+25.2 points, p<0.001). Balse et al.: 93% of LLM logic-error explanations had >=1 correct statement, 50% had >=1 incorrect, 33% missed a logic error. Ahmed et al.: BLEU 1.84 -> 4.58 with repository info, data-flow graph and identifiers in prompt.
limits: Secondary report of other studies; metrics differ.
agent_relevance: Prompt parts that match human strategy cues (repo context, data flow, identifiers) raise explanation quality. Explanations still need verification.

source: Le, Pham, Van, Phan, Phan, Nguyen (2025) When Names Disappear: Revealing What LLMs Actually Understand About Code
finding: Removing or scrambling identifiers (beacons) drops LLM summarization a lot and also hurts execution prediction that should depend only on structure.
numbers: Class summary accuracy GPT-4o 87.3 -> 58.7; Qwen3-Coder 87.2 -> 72.1; DeepSeek V3 87.7 -> 76.7; Llama 4 Maverick 86.2 -> 66.4. Execution pass@1 with identifiers removed: ClassEval 85.7 -> 76.1, LiveCodeBench 85.4 -> 71.2. Llama 4 Maverick LiveCodeBench ambiguity renaming 80.2 -> 56.4.
quote: Surprisingly, we also observe consistent reductions on execution tasks that should depend only on structure
limits: Small execution subsets (37 and 96 samples), GPT-4o as summary judge, only name-based obfuscation; paper has an internal numeric inconsistency.
agent_relevance: Direct LLM analogue of the beacon finding (Brooks). Models lean on names and memorized name-output links. Scaffold: rename or mask identifiers on a second pass to test whether a reading survives.

source: Le, Nguyen, Nguyen (2026) Do Machines Struggle Where Humans Do? LLM and Human Comprehension of Obfuscated Code
finding: Reasoning-tuned LLMs find the same obfuscation levels hard as human programmers; instruction- and coder-tuned models do not.
numbers: Five obfuscation tiers, Block Model levels (atom, block, relational, macro). Reasoning models: significant alignment with human difficulty across experience levels; instruction/coder models: near-zero correlation. CoT trace length tracks difficulty. Control-flow flattening cost scales with state-space size.
limits: Abstract page only: N of humans, model list and exact numbers not read.
agent_relevance: Suggests reasoning traces are where human-like comprehension difficulty appears; a long trace is a difficulty signal the program can count (fits counted steps).

source: Chen, Pan, Hu, Li, Li, Xia (2024/2025) Reasoning Runtime Behavior of a Program with LLM: How Far Are We? (REval)
finding: Models are poor at tracing run-time states, the core of the mental simulation step in bottom-up comprehension.
numbers: 15 models. Average accuracy 44.4%; Incremental Consistency 10.3. GPT-4-Turbo: coverage 88.4, state 71.4, path 57.7, output 82.6, average 75.0, IC 42.5. GPT-3.5-Turbo average 55.7, IC 20.6. Execution-path task averaged 19.4%. CoT on CodeLlama-7B-Instruct: IC 4.1 -> 7.5, path 10.8 -> 21.4, output down.
quote: most LLMs show unsatisfactory performance on both Runtime Behavior Reasoning
limits: Python only (HumanEval, ClassEval); GPT models run once; older models.
agent_relevance: Models often get the final output right without the intermediate states. Do not accept an output claim as proof of understanding; check the trace states with real execution.

source: Liu, Chen, Jabbarvand (2025) Assessing Coherency and Consistency of Code Execution Reasoning by LLMs
finding: LLMs simulate execution plausibly but often wrongly, and shortcut through names; success on bug tasks often looks like pattern matching.
numbers: 16 LLMs on HumanEval. 81.42% of simulations coherent; of those only 46.92% had correct output. Consistency across different-path tests: strong 5.76%, weak 45.37%, random 48.87%. 361 correct outputs flagged as suspicious. GPT-4 25% and DeepSeek-R1 24.9% incoherent.
quote: CES introduces the notion of coherence to determine whether the simulation complies with commonsense execution logic
limits: HumanEval only (164 small programs); loops, conditionals, returns only; 52 programs for the path-consistency test.
agent_relevance: Matches Gilmore's point that reconstruction from a spec is not the same as tracing. Use executed traces, not model-simulated ones, when the agent must understand behaviour.

source: Kang et al. (2023) Explainable Automated Debugging via LLM-driven Scientific Debugging (AutoSD)
finding: LLM loop of hypothesis, debugger experiment, observation, conclusion before patching; a computed analogue of human hypothesis-driven debugging.
numbers: Defects4J correct fixes: v1.2 LLM-Base 87, AutoSD 76; v2.0 110 vs 113. Real execution results: <DONE>-predicted solutions 12.4 points more likely plausible; with LLM-hallucinated debugger output, 11 points less likely. Per-run plausible rate 73% with debugger vs 63% without. Human study 20 participants (6 professionals): explanations kept judging time but raised patch-judgment accuracy on 5 of 6 bugs; 70% wanted explanations, 55% satisfied.
limits: Small human study; benchmark leakage concerns; repair accuracy roughly equal to the plain LLM.
agent_relevance: Direct match for S1/S2 plus a debugger. Key lesson: the loop only helps when observations are real, not model-simulated. Adopt: hypothesis, prediction, run, conclude.

source: Bouzenia and Pradel (2025) Understanding Software Engineering Agents: A Study of Thought-Action-Result Trajectories
finding: Study of 120 agent trajectories from RepairAgent, AutoCodeRover, OpenHands: action mix, length and thought-action coherence.
numbers: 2,822 LLM interactions; mean success ~27%. Action shares: generate fix 23%, run tests 19%, search 15%, explore 14%. RepairAgent iterations: success mean 22 vs failure 40. Action repetition RepairAgent 6.1% (success) vs 13.6% (fail); AutoCodeRover 0.0% vs 8.8%. Thought-action misalignment 1.3-3.7% overall; OpenHands 0.5% (success) vs 1.4% (fail).
quote: Even a single misalignment between thought and action can cause failure or increase computational cost.
limits: Only three agents; underlying models mostly unnamed; ~10 successes per agent; qualitative coding.
agent_relevance: Agents spend only ~29% of actions reading code (search+explore). Repetition and untested fixes are detectable failure signals the program can count.

source: Majgaonkar, Fei, Li, Sarro, Ye (2025) Understanding Code Agent Behaviour: Success and Failure Trajectories
finding: Agents mostly find the right file even when they fail; failure is longer, wider-spread trajectories, and success does not need exact localization.
numbers: File-level match: success 92-97%, failure 59-81% (OpenHands, SWE-agent, Prometheus on SWE-bench Lite/Verified). Function-level match in successes only ~21-34%. Mean steps, OpenHands Verified: 54.05 success vs 98.62 failure; Prometheus Verified 146.59 vs 220.92.
quote: Failed trajectories are longer and have a wider distribution than successful ones.
limits: Trajectory counts not given; different models per agent; approximate-patch claim is correlational.
agent_relevance: Reading breadth is not the bottleneck at file level. A step cap that tightens with a stuck signal is well supported: long runs rarely succeed.

source: Zhang et al. (2026) SWE-Explore: Benchmarking How Coding Agents Explore Repositories
finding: Isolates the reading phase: agent explorers beat retrieval, but line-level coverage is the weak spot and tracks downstream repair.
numbers: 848 issues, 10 languages, 203 repos; K=5 regions, 500-line budget. Line recall: Oracle 0.953, CoSIL 0.788, AutoCodeRover 0.233, Codex 0.194, OpenHands 0.179, Claude Code 0.154, BM25 0.021, Random 0.004. File hit: Claude Code 0.667, CoSIL 0.544. Resolve rate: Random 4.7%, Claude Code 48.0%, CoSIL 59.3%, Oracle 59.7%. Context efficiency vs resolve rate r=0.950.
quote: Despite strong file-level hit rates and ranking scores, most non-oracle explorers still have low F1
limits: Ground truth = what past successful agents read, so alternative valid paths are missed; v1 preprint.
agent_relevance: Iterative code-graph search (CoSIL) reads the right lines far more completely than general agents. Good target for S1: a graph-guided read step and a recall check before editing.

source: Xia, Deng, Dunn, Zhang (2024) Agentless: Demystifying LLM-based Software Engineering Agents
finding: A fixed top-down pipeline (file, then class/function skeleton, then edit lines) matches complex agents at low cost: a coded version of top-down localization.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite 32.00% (96 fixes) at $0.70 per issue. File-level localization: prompting 78.67%, embedding 70.33%, combined 81.67%. Related elements: skeleton 58.33% vs full file 53.67% (and cheaper). Edit locations 49.67%. Reproduction tests: majority vote only 25.67%, plus regression tests 27.00%, plus reproduction tests 32.00%.
quote: Agentless follows a simple three phase process: localization, repair, and patch validation.
limits: Lite benchmark with problem-quality issues (author built Lite-S); only 300 issues; fixed pipeline not tested on novel repos.
agent_relevance: Coarse-to-fine reading with a skeleton view beats showing whole files. Fits 'program decides step order'.

source: Chen, Tang, Deng, Wu, Wu, Jiang, Prasanna, Cohan, Wang (2025) LocAgent: Graph-Guided LLM Agents for Code Localization
finding: Parsing the repo into a graph (directory, file, class, function; contain, import, invoke, inherit edges) and giving the model search/traverse tools improves localization, a call-chain reading aid.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite file Acc@5: LocAgent (Claude-3.5) 94.16% vs 90.15% best baseline; function Acc@5 86.50% vs 83.21%. Loc-Bench file Acc@5 83.39% vs Agentless 67.50%. Fine-tuned Qwen2.5-32B about same level at about 86% lower cost. Removing SearchEntity: 88.32% -> 68.98%.
quote: Converting a graph into a tree structure encodes topology through the spatial distance between entity names.
limits: Python only; Loc-Bench weak on non-bug issues; ablation on a 7B model.
agent_relevance: Hands the model a map to follow call edges, like data-flow building. A deterministic graph tool is cheap and strong.

source: Yang, Jimenez, Wettig, Lieret, Yao, Narasimhan, Press (2024) SWE-agent: Agent-Computer Interfaces
finding: How code is shown to the model changes results: a 100-line window and summarized search beat full file and iterative search.
numbers: SWE-bench Lite (GPT-4 Turbo): 100-line viewer 18.0%, 30-line 14.3%, full file 12.7%; summarized search 18.0%, iterative search 12.0%, no search 15.7%; last-5 observations 18.0% vs full history 15.0%. A failed edit cut eventual success from 90.5% to 57.2%. Successful runs median 12 steps vs 21 for unsuccessful.
quote: Simple commands with a few options and concise documentation are easier for agents to use
limits: Tuned on GPT-4 Turbo; only two models performed well; small ablations on 300 tasks.
agent_relevance: Chunk size and observation history are tunable reading controls. Iterative search made agents step through every match, the opposite of an as-needed strategy.

source: Zhang et al. (2025) EyeMulator: Improving Code Language Models by Mimicking Human Visual Attention
finding: Fine-tuning code models with human eye-tracking priors on loss weights improved all tested configurations.
numbers: 6 backbones, 2 data regimes, 3 CodeXGLUE tasks: all 36 model-task-setting cells had positive matched-metric deltas; gains largest on completion/translation, smaller on summarization.
limits: Abstract page only; no delta magnitudes seen; requires training, so outside our no-training scope.
agent_relevance: Human gaze is a usable signal, but our agent is scaffold-only. Would need to be turned into a read-order prompt, untested.

source: Kaufman et al. (2026) -- comment quality and anchoring
finding: With a docstring present, participants rarely read bottom-up; comments alone did not let them expose wrong postconditions.
numbers: 31/50 top-down; accuracy was lower with incomplete explanations (54.3% vs 62.7% overall in one comparison).
limits: Exploratory; one task type.
agent_relevance: If the agent is given a spec, spec-first reading will anchor it. Insert a code-first pass to break anchoring and compare both readings.

source: Qiao et al. (2025) -- novice and expert strategy framing
finding: Review states that novices lean on bottom-up reading and experienced developers on top-down reading using beacons and cues.
numbers: Background statement; no new measurement. Based on 31 reviewed papers (2022-2024).
limits: Background claim citing older work (Brooks, Letovsky, von Mayrhauser and Vans); not tested here.
agent_relevance: An agent without domain knowledge behaves like a novice; give it explicit beacons (names, types, docstrings) to read first.

source: Lehmen et al. (2026) -- background: classical models hard to operationalize
finding: States that developers switch between bottom-up and top-down comprehension, and that classical theories are hard to turn into predictive models.
numbers: Related work in paper: complexity metrics show only weak correlations with observed human comprehension; prior review by Wyrich et al. covers 95 articles.
limits: Intro claims, not new data.
agent_relevance: Confirms the gap: no existing system implements the von Mayrhauser-Vans integrated model as an LLM loop; our scaffold would be a first operational version.

source: Session search result: no LLM study implements Letovsky or von Mayrhauser-Vans strategy switching directly
finding: Search this session found no paper that tests von Mayrhauser-Vans or Letovsky as an explicit agent prompt. Closest: top-down file-to-function localization (Agentless), graph search (LocAgent, CoSIL), hypothesis debugging (AutoSD).
numbers: Search-based negative: 8 web searches and many fetches, zero direct hits. The arXiv and Semantic Scholar APIs returned 429 (rate limited).
limits: Absence of evidence under limited search.
agent_relevance: Gap to fill: test a strategy-switching scaffold (top-down from spec, bottom-up when a beacon fails, as-needed jumps) and measure it on SWE-Explore-style line recall.
